summary: Defines new states and status tags for the IETF Datatracker so working group chairs can show the progress of working group Internet-Drafts. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6174 defines labels for showing where a working-group Internet-Draft stands, from consideration for adoption through submission to the IESG. Separate annotation tags explain blockers without changing the draft's main state.

questions: what are ietf working group document states
how does datatracker track draft status
what does it mean when a draft is adopted by a wg
what does adopted by a wg mean
subtitle: States and annotation tags for tracking working-group Internet-Drafts.

tldr.problem: The Datatracker already tracked I-D availability and IESG review, but offered little detail about a working group's progress before a draft reached the IESG.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6174 defines working-group draft states, status annotation tags, and an intended maturity level so chairs or delegates can record progress and blockers.
tldr.outcome: The states and tags describe administrative progress. Chairs may use the states that fit their workflow, and the diagram does not define every possible transition.

today: RFC 6174 is Informational and the supplied metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: What the Datatracker Did Not Show
sections.content:
The Datatracker could report whether an Internet-Draft was active, expired, replaced, or submitted to the IESG. It had little ability to show what was happening while a working group was considering and developing a draft.

RFC 6174 defines working-group states to make that progress visible. These states are separate from availability states and from the IESG states that apply after a publication request.
sections.plainLanguage: A label such as Active does not explain whether a group is considering a draft, developing it, or waiting for work. The new states provide a more specific view of that process.

sections.title: Working-Group Draft States
sections.content:
The state sequence can begin with Call for Adoption by WG Issued, followed by states such as Adopted by a WG and WG Document. Later states include In WG Last Call, WG Consensus: Waiting for Writeup, and Submitted to IESG for Publication. A draft can also be parked or declared dead.

The diagram shows common transitions, not every allowed transition. Chairs may move a draft between states as appropriate. The Datatracker was specified to move some drafts automatically, including a version-00 working-group draft approved for posting and a draft entering the IESG Publication Requested state.
sections.plainLanguage: The labels track a draft as a group considers, develops, reviews, and submits it. Chairs can use the states that match their process, including states that show a draft is paused or abandoned.

sections.title: Annotation Tags for Blockers
sections.content:
Annotation tags describe conditions affecting a draft or actions needed to move it forward. Examples include awaiting expert review, needing an author or editor, waiting for a referenced document, or needing a revision after a working-group last call.

Tags do not change the draft's main state. A draft may have multiple tags at once, and a tag should be removed when the condition it describes has been resolved.
sections.plainLanguage: A tag adds a note about what is holding up a draft or what work remains. The draft keeps the same main state while the tag provides extra detail.

sections.title: Maturity Level and Security
sections.content:
Before submission to the IESG, a working-group draft needs an intended maturity level. The RFC lists Experimental, Informational, Best Current Practice, Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, Standard, and Historic.

RFC 6174 is an administrative description of Datatracker state and tags. It proposes no new Internet mechanism and says it has no security implications for the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: A draft also needs a stated publication maturity before IESG submission. These tracking labels describe the IETF process and do not change how Internet protocols work.
